problems.title: Product of geometric-progression terms
problems.question: Find the product of the first n terms of a geometric progression with first term b1 and common ratio q.
problems.idea: Multiply all copies of the first term and add the exponents of q.
steps: The product is $b_1(b_1q)(b_1q^2)\cdots(b_1q^{n-1})$.
There are n copies of b1. The q exponents add to n(n-1)/2.

problems.title: The middle term of a geometric progression
problems.question: The product of the third and seventh terms of a real geometric progression is a. Find its fifth term.
problems.idea: Equidistant geometric terms multiply to the square of their middle term.
steps: The condition gives b5²=a, so a is nonnegative for real terms.
Taking square roots gives b5=√a or b5=-√a. The data do not fix its sign.

problems.title: Collinear coordinate vectors
problems.question: For which n are vectors (3,3-n) and (n+1,-4) collinear?
problems.idea: Their two-dimensional determinant must be zero.
steps: Expand to $n^2-2n-15=0$.
Factor as (n-5)(n+3)=0.

problems.title: Circumradius of a triangle inside a square
problems.question: A square has side 4. Join the midpoints of two adjacent sides to each other and to the opposite square vertex. Find the circumradius of the resulting triangle.
problems.idea: Use coordinates to get the three sides and its area.
formulas: Coordinate triangle area is half the absolute cross product of two side vectors.
steps: Choose the triangle vertices M=(2,0), N=(0,2), C=(4,4).
The sides are MN=2√2 and MC=NC=2√5.
The side vectors from M are (-2,2) and (2,4), whose cross product is -12. Thus the area is 6.
The radius is $(2\sqrt2)(2\sqrt5)^2/(4\cdot6)=5\sqrt2/3=10/(3\sqrt2)$.

problems.title: Sum alternating odd powers
problems.question: Sum $x-x^3+x^5-\cdots-x^{199}$.
problems.idea: This is a finite geometric series with 100 terms and ratio -x².
steps: The exponents are 1,3,...,199, so there are 100 terms.
Use first term x and ratio -x²: $S=x[1-(-x^2)^{100}]/(1+x^2)$.
The even exponent gives $(-x^2)^{100}=x^{200}$, so the numerator is x-x²⁰¹.
For real x the denominator 1+x² is never zero.

problems.title: Arithmetic terms become geometric after additions
problems.question: Three positive numbers form an arithmetic progression with sum 21. Adding 2,3,9 respectively makes an increasing geometric progression. Find its ratio.
problems.idea: Write the original terms symmetrically around their mean seven.
formulas: Three geometric terms u,v,w satisfy v²=uw.
steps: The new terms are 9-d,10,16+d. Thus $100=(9-d)(16+d)=144-7d-d^2$.
This gives d²+7d-44=(d-4)(d+11)=0.
The root d=-11 makes an original term negative, so reject it. The valid root is d=4.
The new sequence is 5,10,20, which has ratio 2.

problems.title: Sum the roots after a substitution
problems.question: Find the sum of the real roots of $\frac7{(x+3)(x-2)}+\frac4{(x+4)(x-3)}=1$.
problems.idea: Both denominators depend on the same expression x²+x.
formulas: Let t=x²+x; denominators become t-6 and t-12.
For x²+x-t=0, the two roots have sum -1.
steps: The original equation excludes x=-3,2,-4,3.
In t, clear denominators: $7(t-12)+4(t-6)=(t-6)(t-12)$. This gives t²-29t+180=(t-9)(t-20)=0.
For t=9, the two real x-roots are (-1±√37)/2. For t=20 they are 4,-5. None is excluded.
Each pair has sum -1, so the combined sum is -2.

problems.title: Square and octagon in one circle
problems.question: A regular octagon inscribed in a circle has area Q. Find the area of a square inscribed in the same circle.
problems.idea: Express both polygon areas using their common circumradius.
steps: The octagon area is Q=4R²sin45°=2√2R².
The square area is 2R² because its diagonals both equal 2R.
Thus the square area divided by Q is 1/√2.

problems.title: Overlap of two equal circles
problems.question: Two circles each have radius R, and their centres are R apart. Find their common area.
problems.idea: The overlap is two identical circular segments with central angle 120°.
steps: Each intersection point and the two centres form an equilateral triangle. The two radii to the intersection points therefore enclose 120° at either centre.
One segment has area $\pi R^2/3-(R^2/2)\sin120^\circ=R^2(\pi/3-\sqrt3/4)$.
The overlap contains two such segments.

problems.title: Keep a hole in a simplified inequality
problems.question: Solve $(x^2-6x+8)/(x-4)\ge0$.
problems.idea: Cancel the common factor while retaining the excluded input.
steps: The original denominator excludes x=4.
For x≠4 the expression equals x-2. The inequality gives x≥2.
Remove the original forbidden value 4 from that interval.

problems.title: An absolute-value fraction greater than two
problems.question: Solve $\left|\frac{1-x}{3x+1}\right|>2$.
problems.idea: Square the comparison after excluding the denominator zero.
steps: Exclude x=-1/3.
The inequality becomes $(1-x)^2-4(3x+1)^2>0$.
Factor: (-7x-1)(5x+3)>0, equivalently (7x+1)(5x+3)<0.
The solution is between the two zeros -3/5 and -1/7, excluding -1/3.

problems.title: Recognise a nested radical
problems.question: Evaluate $(8+\sqrt{60})(\sqrt{10}-\sqrt6)\sqrt{4-\sqrt{15}}$.
problems.idea: The final square root is half of the preceding radical difference.
steps: The radical difference is positive, so it equals twice the principal final square root.
The expression becomes $(8+2\sqrt{15})(16-4\sqrt{15})/2$.

problems.title: Equal displacement vectors
problems.question: For A=(0,1), B=(1,0), C=(1,2), D=(2,1), identify the equal vectors among the listed choices.
problems.idea: Subtract starting coordinates from ending coordinates.
steps: AB=(1,-1), and CD=(2-1,1-2)=(1,-1), so those vectors are equal.
For the other choices: AC=(1,1) differs from AD=(2,0); BC=(0,2) differs from AD; CA=(-1,-1) differs from DA=(-2,0); CB=(0,-2) differs from DA; DC=(-1,1) differs from AD.

problems.title: Length of a linear combination of vectors
problems.question: For vectors a=(3,2) and b=(0,-1), find the length of -2a+4b.
problems.idea: Perform the vector arithmetic coordinate by coordinate, then use the Euclidean length formula.
steps: The length is √(36+64)=10.

problems.title: Find an arithmetic progression’s first term
problems.question: For arithmetic progression an, the partial sums satisfy S2-S5+a2=8 and S3+a3=17. Find a1.
problems.idea: Express each partial sum and term using the first term A and difference d.
steps: The first condition becomes (2A+d)-(5A+10d)+(A+d)=8, giving A+4d=-4.
The second becomes (3A+3d)+(A+2d)=17, giving 4A+5d=17.
Multiply the first by 4 and subtract the second: 11d=-33, so d=-3.

problems.title: Sum odd numbers in a specified interval
problems.question: Find the sum of all odd integers from 112 through 138 inclusive.
problems.idea: They form an arithmetic progression from 113 to 137.
steps: The odd terms are 113,115,...,137, with count (137-113)/2+1=13.
Their mean is (113+137)/2=125.
The sum is 13·125=1625.

problems.title: Angle between two vectors from a centroid
problems.question: A triangle has vertices A=(2,1), B=(1,5), C=(3,3). Let O be its centroid. Find the cosine of the angle between OA and OB.
problems.idea: Average the vertex coordinates to find O, then use the dot product.
steps: OA=(0,-2), OB=(-1,2). Their dot product is -4.
The lengths are 2 and √5, so the cosine is -4/(2√5)=-2/√5.

problems.title: Dot products of perpendicular unit vectors
problems.question: Vectors a,b are perpendicular unit vectors. Evaluate $(3a+2b)\cdot(a-b)$.
problems.idea: Distribute the dot product and use the unit and perpendicular conditions.
steps: Expand to 3(a·a)-3(a·b)+2(b·a)-2(b·b).
Substitute the four known values to get 3-0+0-2=1.

problems.title: Area of a triangle inside a right trapezoid
problems.question: In right trapezoid ABCD, angles A and B are right. Given AD=8, BC=4, CD=5, find the area of triangle ACD.
problems.idea: The sloping leg and the base difference determine the height.
steps: The horizontal difference of the bases is 8-4=4.
The height is √(5²-4²)=3.
Triangle ACD has base AD=8 and the same height, so its area is 8·3/2=12.

problems.title: A bound on the sum of squared roots
problems.question: Find q for which $x^2-6x+q=0$ has two distinct real roots whose squares sum to less than 26.
problems.idea: Use the discriminant for distinctness and Vieta’s formulas for the squared sum.
formulas: D=36-4q; root sum 6 and root product q.
steps: D>0 requires q<9.
The squared sum is 36-2q<26, requiring q>5.
Intersect to obtain 5<q<9.
problems.answer: $q\in(5,9)$ (option გ), when the two roots must be distinct.
problems.note: If a repeated root is counted twice, q=9 also works: both roots are 3 and their squares sum to 18. The printed option uses the distinct-root interpretation.

problems.title: Both roots strictly positive, including the boundary case
problems.question: For which a are both real roots of $x^2-x+a=0$ positive?
problems.idea: The roots have sum one. A positive product makes them the same sign, and the discriminant controls reality.
formulas: Root sum 1; root product a; discriminant D=1-4a.
steps: The roots are real if a≤1/4.
They are both positive if their product a>0, since their positive sum then rules out two negative roots.
Thus 0<a≤1/4 if a repeated positive root is allowed. At a=1/4 the root is 1/2 twice.
If two distinct roots are required, the upper bound becomes strict.
problems.answer: $0<a\le1/4$ allowing a repeated root; $0<a<1/4$ for distinct roots (printed option ე).
problems.note: The wording does not explicitly say “distinct.” The printed strict upper bound omits the valid repeated positive root at a=1/4 unless distinctness is intended.

problems.title: An arc between two tangency points in a right angle
problems.question: A semicircle is inscribed in a right triangle, with its diameter on the hypotenuse and its arc tangent to both legs. Under the intended interpretation that its centre divides the hypotenuse into lengths 15 and 20, find the arc length between the two leg-contact points.
problems.idea: The centre lies on the right-angle bisector. Use that bisector ratio to find the triangle, then the circle radius.
formulas: Angle-bisector theorem: the adjacent legs have ratio 15:20=3:4.
A 3:4 right triangle has hypotenuse ratio 5.
For legs p,q on coordinate axes, their hypotenuse line is x/p+y/q=1.
steps: The hypotenuse is 15+20=35, so the legs are 21 and 28.
The centre is equally distant r from the two perpendicular legs, so it has coordinates (r,r). Since it is on the hypotenuse, r/21+r/28=1, giving r=12.
The radii to the contact points are perpendicular, so the shorter arc between them has angle 90°.
Its length is one quarter of 2πr, namely 6π.
problems.note: The source says the “diameter” divides the hypotenuse into two lengths, but does not identify the dividing point. A diameter is a segment, not a dividing point. The intended centre division gives the listed answer; the interpretation is stated explicitly here.

problems.title: A shifted combination of geometric terms
problems.question: For a geometric progression bn, $b_2+b_5-b_4=10$ and $b_3+b_6-b_5=20$. Find the common ratio.
problems.idea: The second combination is the first multiplied by the common ratio.
steps: Thus 20=10q, giving q=2. The first combination is nonzero, so division by 10 is valid.

problems.title: A term compared with its infinite tail
problems.question: In a convergent geometric progression, every term is four times the sum of all later terms. Find the ratio.
problems.idea: Express the infinite tail after a term using the geometric-series formula.
formulas: For |q|<1, the tail after a nonzero term b is bq/(1-q).
steps: The condition is b=4bq/(1-q).
Cancel nonzero b: 1-q=4q, giving 5q=1.
Thus q=1/5, which satisfies |q|<1 and makes the tail b/4.

problems.title: Length of a sum using its angle
problems.question: Vectors a,b have lengths 2 and 3 and enclose 60°. Find the length of a+2b.
problems.idea: Expand the squared norm using the dot product.
steps: The squared length is 4+4·9+4·3=52.
Take the positive square root: √52=2√13.
